title: Email Tracking-Pixel Detector
metaDescription: Paste an email's source or drop a .eml file to find hidden tracking pixels, click-tracking links and the platform that sent it. Runs entirely in your browser.
description: Find out whether an email reports back to its sender when you open it. Paste the raw source or drop a .eml file to reveal hidden tracking pixels, click-tracking redirects and the marketing platform behind the message.

educational.howItWorks: The detector parses the raw message the way a mail client does: it reads the header block, walks every MIME part (including nested multipart/alternative and multipart/mixed containers), and decodes quoted-printable and base64 bodies so the real HTML is visible. It then inspects every tag for the signatures of an open-tracking beacon — width or height of two pixels or less, inline styles that hide the image (display:none, visibility:hidden, opacity:0), open-tracking style paths, and hosts that belong to more than forty known email-marketing and sales-tracking services. Each is checked for click-tracking wrappers, either by matching those same vendor domains or by spotting redirect-style hosts and paths; where the true destination is visible inside the wrapper (a URL or base64 query parameter, or an encoded path segment) it is decoded and shown. Finally, delivery headers such as X-Mailer, List-Unsubscribe, Feedback-ID, X-SG-EID, X-MC-*, X-SES-* and the bounce/Return-Path domain are weighed together to name the sending platform. Nothing is fetched: the images and links are only read as text, so running the check never triggers the trackers it finds.
tips: Turn off automatic remote-image loading in your mail client, or use a provider that proxies images — that single setting defeats nearly every open-tracking pixel
Hover over links before clicking; if the visible domain does not match the destination shown in the status bar, the click is being logged through a redirect
Copy the full source from "Show original" or "View source" rather than the rendered page — the headers are where the sending platform gives itself away
A tiny, hidden or vendor-hosted image is a strong signal, but any remote image can be used to infer an open; treat "remote images" as a soft warning, not a pass
When a message from an individual contains a sales-tracking pixel, replying via a fresh plain-text email avoids feeding their read receipts
commonMistakes: Assuming a plain-looking personal email cannot track you — sales add-ons inject one-pixel beacons into ordinary one-to-one messages
Opening the email to "check" it in a normal client with images enabled, which fires the pixel before you have inspected anything
Judging a link by its anchor text instead of its actual href — wrapped links look identical until you read the source
Pasting only the rendered text of the message, which strips the HTML and hides both pixels and redirect wrappers
Trusting that unsubscribing removes tracking; the unsubscribe link itself usually carries a per-recipient identifier
